attempts.answer:
Below is an evidence‑based framework to distinguish dengue‑induced vascular leak with pulmonary edema from iatrogenic fluid overload at initial presentation, organized around timing, hemodynamics, clinical/laboratory features, and bedside imaging. The approach emphasizes early recognition of dengue warning signs, careful history of fluid exposure, and serial monitoring guided by ultrasound and vital signs.

Key principles and timelines
- Dengue capillary leak typically emerges after the febrile phase, with warning signs and clinical evidence of plasma leakage (third spacing such as pleural/ascites effusions) preceding frank shock; pulmonary edema may develop during the critical phase when systemic vascular permeability is elevated. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">In severe dengue, capillary leak produces profound shock and pulmonary edema during days 2–6 after dengue onset in adults</cite> and <cite id="39a6fdf1-4">pleural effusion appears early in the critical phase as fluid accumulation from increased capillary permeability</cite>. 
- Iatrogenic fluid overload usually occurs after transfusion or resuscitation in patients at risk of plasma leakage. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">A patient with an underlying lung malignancy developed pulmonary edema on day 16 due to fluid overload from malignant pleural effusion; by contrast, dengue‑related edema occurred earlier with marked hemoconcentration and shock</cite>. 
- Management frameworks explicitly caution that fluid resuscitation is needed to counteract plasma leakage but must be titrated to avoid overload. <cite id="52db8305-0">In dengue shock, intravascular fluid administration counters plasma leakage; inappropriate therapy increases risk of fluid overload and congestive heart failure, while under-resuscitation worsens oxygenation</cite> and <cite id="7a79cc2d-1">WHO and national guidelines recommend an inverted “V” fluid pattern (start low, escalate during the critical phase, taper later), acknowledging empirical basis and the risk that more fluid may worsen third spacing</cite>.

History and hemodynamics at presentation
- Ask specifically about transfusion/recent blood products, IV fluids, diuretics, and baseline heart disease; track 24‑hour fluid balance. <cite id="52db8305-0">Both fluid overload and inadequate resuscitation can worsen oxygenation; point-of-care ultrasound and IVC parameters can guide avoiding excessive fluid in dengue</cite>. 
- Look for dengue shock physiology: profound hypotension (especially post‑febrile), postural fall in systolic BP, and tachycardia with narrow pulse pressure. <cite id="39a6fdf1-1">Postural hypotension reflects intravascular volume reduction from capillary leak and had sensitivity 87% and specificity 82.7% for predicting severe dengue in prospective testing</cite>. 
- Early warning signs beyond tachypnea/dyspnea: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, lethargy, mucosal bleeding, hepatomegaly, and increasing hematocrit with falling platelets. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">WHO classifies warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy/restlessness, liver enlargement, and increase in hematocrit with rapid fall in platelets)</cite> and <cite id="39a6fdf1-3">warning signs have moderate-to-good performance for ruling out progression to severe dengue; decision-tree models using postural hypotension and pleural/ascites had diagnostic odds ratio 53.9</cite>. 
- Distinguish fever phase versus recovery phase: tachypnea and hypoxemia early in shock with rising hematocrit and effusions are consistent with capillary leak; tachypnea with rising jugular venous pressure, distended neck veins, and signs of cardiac decompensation after transfusion/fluids suggest overload. <cite id="7a79cc2d-0">Capillary leak is the hallmark of severe dengue with timing and hemoconcentration</cite>.

Physical exam and fluid accumulation
- Inspect for peripheral edema, pleural/ascites signs, and dependent crackles; palpate for hepatomegaly and hypovolemic/pulmonary exam paradoxes. <cite id="39a6fdf1-4">Accumulation of fluid in tissues (ascites, pleural effusion) is a manifestation of plasma leakage due to increased capillary permeability at the start of the critical phase</cite>. 
- Look for distributive shock features without classic cardiac decompensation (warm periphery, delayed capillary refill) in early capillary leak; contrast with cardiogenic shock signs (cold periphery, weak pulses, elevated JVP) when fluid overload is superimposed. <cite id="52db8305-0">Patients with cardiogenic shock have elevated NT‑proBNP and marked B‑lines on lung ultrasound; IVC ultrasound and POCUS can guide fluid therapy to avoid excess</cite>. 
- Skin turgor and “tenting” in dengue may be poor due to hypoproteinemia from plasma leakage; avoid relying on generalized edema distribution alone. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">Marked hemoconcentration accompanies dengue‑related capillary leak and shock</cite>.

Laboratory markers
- Serial hematocrit is central: a 20% rise from baseline over 6–8 hours confirms plasma leakage by WHO criteria; platelets fall, often precipitating fluid accumulation 24–48 hours before clinical leakage. <cite id="7a79cc2d-2">Clinical hematocrit rise of 20% over 6–8 hours or ultrasound evidence of effusions confirms plasma leakage; platelet drop below 100,000/mm3 precedes leakage by 24–48 hours</cite>. 
- Leukocytosis and bandemia raise suspicion for superimposed infection or stress, which can worsen capillary leak. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">Leukocytosis and bandemia may indicate superimposed bacterial infection or other stressors in severe dengue; massive GI bleeding and bacteremia were major causes of leukocytosis in fatal cases</cite>. 
- Cardiac biomarkers: NT‑proBNP/BNP are elevated in cardiogenic pulmonary edema and correlate with B‑line burden; this supports a cardiac/non‑dengue‑vasculature mechanism when markedly elevated. <cite id="52db8305-0">NT‑proBNP median 970.5 pg/mL in cardiogenic shock; B‑line count correlates strongly with NT‑proBNP (r=0.69) and with acute cardiogenic edema identification (AUROC 0.978 for NT‑proBNP)</cite>.

Bedside imaging and ultrasound
- Chest X‑ray: noncardiogenic (dengue‑like) edema shows bilateral, diffuse, patchy infiltrates with air bronchograms and “Kerley B” lines; cardiogenic edema shows cephalization, Hampton’s lines, and prominent Kerley B lines with cardiomegaly. Distribution and signs of elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure are key discriminators. <cite id="52db8305-2">Cardiogenic pulmonary edema exhibits cephalization and broad vascular pedicle with peri-bronchovascular “septal” (Kerley B) lines; noncardiogenic edema presents diffuse bilateral infiltrates with air bronchograms, not specific but characteristic</cite>. 
- Lung ultrasound (POCUS) is more sensitive than symptoms/radiography for cardiogenic edema and quantifies extravascular lung water via B‑lines. It can also detect pleural fluid and assess IVC collapsibility to gauge fluid responsiveness. <cite id="52db8305-2">Transthoracic ultrasound detects pulmonary edema via B‑lines representing alveolar‑interstitial fluid; B‑line number correlates with extravascular lung water and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure</cite> and <cite id="52db8305-0">BLUE/FALLS protocols use B‑lines to differentiate cardiogenic from other shock; POCUS of IVC and lung ultrasound can guide fluid management in dengue</cite>. 
- Anterior chest alone can miss lateral zone pathology; include lateral decubitus views to reduce sensitivity loss in ED settings. <cite id="52db8305-1">Limiting lung ultrasound to the anterior chest misses up to 16.5% of ADHF cases; adding lateral views improves detection</cite>. 
- Distribution matters: diffuse B‑lines across multiple zones support noncardiogenic edema (capillary leak/ARDS), focal B‑lines and pleural effusion with septic features suggest infection; cardiogenic patterns localize to dependent bases with IVC distension and cardiomegaly on CXR. <cite id="52db8305-4">Diffuse multiple B‑lines appear in noncardiogenic edema (ARDS, pneumonia); focal B‑lines are common in pneumonia, contusion, infarction, malignancy</cite> and <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">clinical fluid accumulation (effusions) is a dengue warning sign with marked hemoconcentration</cite>.

Clinical reasoning at initial presentation
- Suggestive of dengue‑induced capillary leak/pulmonary edema:
  - Early post‑febrile (within 5–10 days), febrile chart shows typical DF course; new tachypnea/dyspnea with hypoxemia; hypotension/postural drop; abdominal pain or hepatomegaly; persistent vomiting; lethargy; mucosal bleeding; rising hematocrit (20% within 6–8 h) with falling platelets; pleural/ascites on exam or FAST-like ultrasound; CXR shows bilateral patchy infiltrates with air bronchograms; ultrasound shows diffuse B‑lines across lung fields with low IVC pressure; BNP modestly elevated or not diagnostic for heart failure. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">Dengue pulmonary edema occurred during days 5–6 post‑onset with marked hemoconcentration and profound shock</cite>, <cite id="39a6fdf1-4">pleural effusion appears early in critical phase from capillary leak</cite>, <cite id="39a6fdf1-1">postural hypotension predicts severe dengue with high sensitivity/specificity</cite>, <cite id="7a79cc2d-2">hematocrit rise of 20% confirms plasma leakage; platelet drop precedes it</cite>, <cite id="52db8305-2">noncardiogenic edema patterns on imaging</cite>, <cite id="52db8305-0">lung ultrasound and IVC assessment guide fluid therapy</cite>.
- Suggestive of iatrogenic fluid overload:
  - Recent transfusion(s) with fresh plasma/packed cells or large crystalloids; positive fluid balance of liters in 24–48 hours; tachypnea with hypoxemia despite or after diuretics; rising JVP/neck vein distension, distant heart sounds, bibasilar crackles; CXR shows patchy infiltrates with signs of cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion; lung ultrasound shows prominent B‑lines with possible pleural fluid and non‑collapsible IVC; BNP markedly elevated with clinical sepsis/ARDS superimposed. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">Effusion‑related fluid overload caused pulmonary edema on day 16 in a patient with malignant pleural effusion</cite>, <cite id="52db8305-0">inappropriate fluid therapy increases fluid overload; POCUS can detect fluid overload signs</cite>, <cite id="52db8305-2">IVC collapse indicates fluid overload; ultrasound detects pleural effusions and evaluates IVC</cite>.

Workup and early monitoring plan
- Immediate: oxygenation/saturation, O2 requirement, BP with posture, HR, capillary refill, urine output, hematocrit vs baseline, platelets, white blood cell count with neutrophils/bandemia, and a focused physical and abdominal exam. <cite id="39a6fdf1-1">Postural hypotension’s diagnostic performance supports its use early in dengue</cite> and <cite id="39a6fdf1-3">rise in hematocrit has low sensitivity but high specificity for severe dengue</cite>.
- Imaging: chest radiograph to assess infiltrates and distribution; if equivocal, bedside lung ultrasound with anterior and lateral views, measurement of B‑line counts, pleural effusion search, and IVC collapsibility. <cite id="52db8305-2">B‑line number correlates with extravascular water and predicts outcomes</cite> and <cite id="52db8305-4">diffuse B‑lines favor noncardiogenic edema</cite>. 
- Laboratories: repeat hematocrit/platelets every 4–6 hours; consider BNP/NT‑proBNP if available to quantify cardiac stress; obtain blood cultures if sepsis is suspected based on warning signs. <cite id="52db8305-0">NT‑proBNP levels correlate with B‑lines and identify cardiogenic pulmonary edema</cite> and <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">bacteremia is an important warning sign with high leukocytosis</cite>.

Differential pitfalls and how to avoid
- Overdiagnosing plasma leakage when fluid overload is present: maintain strict fluid balance charts; hold transfusions unless for shock; favor restrictive transfusion thresholds; use POCUS to guide both resuscitation and de‑resuscitation. <cite id="52db8305-0">Inappropriate fluid therapy increases congestive heart failure risk; inverted “V” titration with POCUS reduces overload risk</cite>. 
- Under‑recognizing cardiogenic decompensation in dengue: do not rely solely on hematocrit; evaluate for sepsis, MI, or pre‑existing HF; use BNP and ultrasound to detect cardiac etiologies. <cite id="52db8305-0">Cardiogenic shock in dengue has elevated NT‑proBNP with >30 B‑lines and can mimic plasma leakage</cite>. 
- Under‑recognizing dengue plasma leakage: track hematocrit trends and warning signs; do not wait for massive hemoconcentration. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">Plasma leakage can be suspected even without extreme hematocrit elevation if effusions and hypotensive episodes occur</cite> and <cite id="39a6fdf1-2">significant hematocrit rise may be absent if early fluid intervention alters physiology</cite>.

Practical bedside algorithm at initial presentation
1) Ask history: febrile course, dengue exposure, transfusions/IV fluids in last 24–48 h, baseline cardiac disease. Measure 24 h intake/output. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">Differentiate dengue edema (early post‑febrile) from effusion‑related overload (later with clear exposure)</cite> and <cite id="52db8305-0">track fluid balance and use POCUS to prevent overload</cite>. 
2) Hemodynamics: BP with posture, pulse, JVP, cap refill. Identify postural drop or narrow pulse pressure. <cite id="39a6fdf1-1">Postural fall in SBP >10.33% strongly predicts severe dengue</cite>. 
3) Warning signs: abdominal pain/persistent vomiting, lethargy, mucosal bleeding, hepatomegaly, fluid accumulation, hematocrit trajectory. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">WHO warning signs define risk of plasma leakage/severe dengue</cite> and <cite id="7a79cc2d-2">20% hematocrit rise and platelet drop guide plasma leakage assessment</cite>. 
4) Imaging: chest X‑ray and bedside lung ultrasound (anterior + lateral). Assess distribution and presence of pleural fluid; count B‑lines; evaluate IVC. <cite id="52db8305-2">Diffuse B‑lines across lung zones favor noncardiogenic edema; add lateral views to reduce missed cardiogenic cases</cite> and <cite id="52db8305-0">IVC ultrasound detects fluid overload; B‑line counts correlate with NT‑proBNP</cite>. 
5) Labs: repeat hematocrit/platelets; consider BNP/NT‑proBNP and blood cultures if sepsis suspected; check leukocyte/NEU% for superimposed infection. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">Bandemia indicates superimposed infection/stress in severe dengue</cite> and <cite id="52db8305-0">BNP-guided strategy distinguishes cardiogenic from noncardiogenic edema</cite>. 
6) Early management: 
   - Dengue capillary leak with pulmonary edema: initiate low‑dose isotonic resuscitation per inverted “V,” transfuse packed cells only for shock with clinical hemodynamic monitoring and POCUS; consider RAR if fluid overload signs arise; manage oxygenation and watch for ARDS. <cite id="7a79cc2d-1">Intravascular fluid counters plasma leakage; inverted “V” is recommended but empirical; escalation risks overload</cite> and <cite id="52db8305-0">POCUS and IVC parameters reduce inappropriate fluid and prevent overload</cite>. 
   - Iatrogenic fluid overload: halt non‑urgent IV fluids and transfusions; record fluid balance; give loop diuretics per sepsis/heart failure protocol; re‑assess oxygenation and hemodynamics; reassess hematocrit to detect dilution. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">Effusion‑related fluid overload can cause rapid pulmonary edema</cite> and <cite id="52db8305-0">avoid excessive fluid; ultrasound detects overload and guides therapy</cite>.

Practical tips and red flags
- Dengue vs overload: feverish, febrile chart, warning signs, rising hematocrit with falling platelets, pleural/ascites, hypotension with postural drop, normal or modest BNP and diffuse B‑lines with air bronchograms. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">Hemorrhagic fever with capillary leak and hemoconcentration can precipitate shock and pulmonary edema early post‑fever</cite>, <cite id="7a79cc2d-2">hematocrit/platelet trajectory confirms plasma leakage</cite>, <cite id="52db8305-2">noncardiogenic edema imaging patterns</cite>. 
- Overload vs dengue: recent transfusion/fluids, positive fluid balance in liters, rising JVP, distant heart sounds, cardiomegaly/vascular pedicle on CXR, prominent B‑lines with pleural fluid, non‑collapsible IVC, markedly elevated BNP; consider sepsis/ARDS superimposed. <cite id="52db8305-0">Inappropriate fluid increases congestive heart failure risk; POCUS detects overload</cite> and <cite id="52db8305-2">IVC distension and pleural effusions localize to overload</cite>. 
- Caveats: fluid accumulation without hematocrit rise can occur if early IV fluid therapy alters physiology; conversely, dehydration can falsely lower hematocrit. Track serial hematocrit and ultrasound signs rather than single values. <cite id="39a6fdf1-2">Some cases of leakage lack a large hematocrit rise due to early fluid intervention; dehydration/vomiting can also reduce hematocrit</cite>. 
- Early detection matters: warning signs such as fluid accumulation and postural hypotension identify patients likely to progress to severe disease and need aggressive but monitored resuscitation. <cite id="39a6fdf1-3">Ascites/pleural effusion and postural fall in SBP had good sensitivity/specificity for severe dengue; a decision tree using these had high diagnostic odds</cite>.

Bottom line
- At initial presentation, favor dengue‑induced vascular leak with pulmonary edema when illness is early post‑febrile, with fever history, warning signs, rising hematocrit/platelet fall, effusions, distributive hemodynamics, and noncardiogenic imaging/ultrasound patterns; conversely, favor iatrogenic fluid overload when there is a clear history of transfusion/large IV fluids in the last 24–48 hours, signs of cardiac decompensation with elevated JVP and IVC distension, pleural effusions from overload, and imaging/ultrasound consistent with cardiogenic/non‑collapsible IVC findings. Integrate serial hematocrit, postural BP, warning signs, and POCUS‑guided fluid management to minimize both under‑ and over‑resuscitation. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">Dengue capillary leak and hemoconcentration precipitate shock and pulmonary edema early post‑febrile, whereas effusion‑related overload occurs later</cite> and <cite id="52db8305-0">inappropriate fluid increases overload risk; POCUS of IVC and lung ultrasound differentiates etiologies and guides therapy</cite>. <cite id="7a79cc2d-1">Guidelines recommend titrated fluid resuscitation to prevent overload while maintaining perfusion</cite>.

Snippet: Patients with cardiogenic shock in our study had elevated NT-proBNP, with a median level of 970.5 pg/mL, which is above the level associated with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema among patients aged 75 years [44]. Intravascular fluid administration is the key intervention for dengue shock, serving to counteract plasma leakage from capillaries during the critical phase [3]. An inverted 'V' pattern of fluid therapy is recommended by the WHO SEARO guidelines for patients with dengue, due to dynamic fluid changes during the critical and recovery phases [1]. Inappropriate fluid therapy increases the risk of fluid overload and congestive heart failure among patients with severe plasma leakage [1,3]. However, patients who receive inadequate intravascular fluid administration might progress to shock during the critical phase [1,3]. Both fluid overload and inadequate intravascular volume could lead to worsening of tissue oxygenation, resulting in organ failure among patients with dengue [47]. Our analysis sought to evaluate the sensitivity of the B-profile for ruling out pulmonary edema in the ED patient population.MethodsThe ultrasound lung scans of patients with confirmed official diagnoses of acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) from two ED databases were retrospectively analyzed. 170 acutely dyspneic patients had complete studies (130 from one database and 40 from the other). These 28 patients did not show anterior bilateral B-lines that fit the criteria for positive under the BLUE protocol. Moreover, 25% (7/28) of these missed patients had only lateral B-lines on their lung scans and B-lines would have been detected only by including scans of the lateral zones.ConclusionsLimiting the sonographic lung examination to the anterior chest areas only will miss cases of ADHF in the dyspneic ED patients. Title: Revisiting the fluid requirement during the critical phase of dengue: Does it actually follow a bell-shaped curve?
Snippet: Plasma leakage due to a transient increase in capillary permeability is the hallmark of dengue haemorrhagic fever. There is no specific antiviral agent for dengue. Therefore, the mainstay of management during the plasma leakage phase is the judicious use of intravenous fluid to ensure adequate organ perfusion and to prevent fluid overload. The current practice guidelines for dengue are empirical. They are mostly based on expert opinions. The rates and amounts of fluid to be administered during the critical phase of the disease have not been studied in randomised controlled trials. It is hypothesised that the rate of fluid leakage during the critical phase follows a bell-shaped curve. Based on this concept, both WHO and Sri Lankan guidelines recommend starting fluid at a lower rate, increasing the rate until the midpoint of the CP, and gradually reducing the infusion rate thereafter. However, the authors believe that the more fluid you give during the critical phase, the more will leak out into the third space. Thus increasing the complications of fluid overload without improving the effective plasma volume. Therefore, administering fluids at an escalating rate may be superfluous and could result in fluid overload.
</snippet>

Snippet: Dengue fever, a prevalent tropical viral illness transmitted by mosquitoes, poses a substantial burden on healthcare systems in Southeast Asia. Despite the increase in case density annually there is a noticeable downward trend in mortality rates in Sri Lanka. The pathophysiological hallmark of severe dengue is plasma leakage, leading to potentially life-threatening complications such as shock and organ failure. Key aspects of clinical care include early recognition of warning signs, monitoring of clinical parameters, and tailoring fluid therapy to individual patient needs. Optimizing fluid management is essential for reducing morbidity and mortality associated with severe dengue infection. Key decisions on fluid management are individualized with intense monitoring of vital parameters. The amount and type of fluid administered to maintain adequate perfusion while preventing fluid overload are based on the bed side clinical and sonographic assessment. This case-based discussion provides an overview of current fluid management strategies in various clinical stages of dengue highlighting the common pitfalls that may arise during management of complicated dengue patients. It is of utmost importance that we acquire the insight into the judicious fluid management during critical phase of dengue to minimize morbidity and mortality.

Below is an evidence‑based framework to distinguish dengue‑induced vascular leak with pulmonary edema from iatrogenic fluid overload at initial presentation, organized around timing, hemodynamics, clinical/laboratory features, and bedside imaging. The approach emphasizes early recognition of dengue warning signs, careful history of fluid exposure, and serial monitoring guided by ultrasound and vital signs.

Key principles and timelines
- Dengue capillary leak typically emerges after the febrile phase, with warning signs and clinical evidence of plasma leakage (third spacing such as pleural/ascites effusions) preceding frank shock; pulmonary edema may develop during the critical phase when systemic vascular permeability is elevated. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">In severe dengue, capillary leak produces profound shock and pulmonary edema during days 2–6 after dengue onset in adults</cite> and <cite id="39a6fdf1-4">pleural effusion appears early in the critical phase as fluid accumulation from increased capillary permeability</cite>. 
- Iatrogenic fluid overload usually occurs after transfusion or resuscitation in patients at risk of plasma leakage. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">A patient with an underlying lung malignancy developed pulmonary edema on day 16 due to fluid overload from malignant pleural effusion; by contrast, dengue‑related edema occurred earlier with marked hemoconcentration and shock</cite>. 
- Management frameworks explicitly caution that fluid resuscitation is needed to counteract plasma leakage but must be titrated to avoid overload. <cite id="52db8305-0">In dengue shock, intravascular fluid administration counters plasma leakage; inappropriate therapy increases risk of fluid overload and congestive heart failure, while under-resuscitation worsens oxygenation</cite> and <cite id="7a79cc2d-1">WHO and national guidelines recommend an inverted “V” fluid pattern (start low, escalate during the critical phase, taper later), acknowledging empirical basis and the risk that more fluid may worsen third spacing</cite>.

History and hemodynamics at presentation
- Ask specifically about transfusion/recent blood products, IV fluids, diuretics, and baseline heart disease; track 24‑hour fluid balance. <cite id="52db8305-0">Both fluid overload and inadequate resuscitation can worsen oxygenation; point-of-care ultrasound and IVC parameters can guide avoiding excessive fluid in dengue</cite>. 
- Look for dengue shock physiology: profound hypotension (especially post‑febrile), postural fall in systolic BP, and tachycardia with narrow pulse pressure. <cite id="39a6fdf1-1">Postural hypotension reflects intravascular volume reduction from capillary leak and had sensitivity 87% and specificity 82.7% for predicting severe dengue in prospective testing</cite>. 
- Early warning signs beyond tachypnea/dyspnea: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, lethargy, mucosal bleeding, hepatomegaly, and increasing hematocrit with falling platelets. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">WHO classifies warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy/restlessness, liver enlargement, and increase in hematocrit with rapid fall in platelets)</cite> and <cite id="39a6fdf1-3">warning signs have moderate-to-good performance for ruling out progression to severe dengue; decision-tree models using postural hypotension and pleural/ascites had diagnostic odds ratio 53.9</cite>. 
- Distinguish fever phase versus recovery phase: tachypnea and hypoxemia early in shock with rising hematocrit and effusions are consistent with capillary leak; tachypnea with rising jugular venous pressure, distended neck veins, and signs of cardiac decompensation after transfusion/fluids suggest overload. <cite id="7a79cc2d-0">Capillary leak is the hallmark of severe dengue with timing and hemoconcentration</cite>.

Physical exam and fluid accumulation
- Inspect for peripheral edema, pleural/ascites signs, and dependent crackles; palpate for hepatomegaly and hypovolemic/pulmonary exam paradoxes. <cite id="39a6fdf1-4">Accumulation of fluid in tissues (ascites, pleural effusion) is a manifestation of plasma leakage due to increased capillary permeability at the start of the critical phase</cite>. 
- Look for distributive shock features without classic cardiac decompensation (warm periphery, delayed capillary refill) in early capillary leak; contrast with cardiogenic shock signs (cold periphery, weak pulses, elevated JVP) when fluid overload is superimposed. <cite id="52db8305-0">Patients with cardiogenic shock have elevated NT‑proBNP and marked B‑lines on lung ultrasound; IVC ultrasound and POCUS can guide fluid therapy to avoid excess</cite>. 
- Skin turgor and “tenting” in dengue may be poor due to hypoproteinemia from plasma leakage; avoid relying on generalized edema distribution alone. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">Marked hemoconcentration accompanies dengue‑related capillary leak and shock</cite>.

Laboratory markers
- Serial hematocrit is central: a 20% rise from baseline over 6–8 hours confirms plasma leakage by WHO criteria; platelets fall, often precipitating fluid accumulation 24–48 hours before clinical leakage. <cite id="7a79cc2d-2">Clinical hematocrit rise of 20% over 6–8 hours or ultrasound evidence of effusions confirms plasma leakage; platelet drop below 100,000/mm3 precedes leakage by 24–48 hours</cite>. 
- Leukocytosis and bandemia raise suspicion for superimposed infection or stress, which can worsen capillary leak. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">Leukocytosis and bandemia may indicate superimposed bacterial infection or other stressors in severe dengue; massive GI bleeding and bacteremia were major causes of leukocytosis in fatal cases</cite>. 
- Cardiac biomarkers: NT‑proBNP/BNP are elevated in cardiogenic pulmonary edema and correlate with B‑line burden; this supports a cardiac/non‑dengue‑vasculature mechanism when markedly elevated. <cite id="52db8305-0">NT‑proBNP median 970.5 pg/mL in cardiogenic shock; B‑line count correlates strongly with NT‑proBNP (r=0.69) and with acute cardiogenic edema identification (AUROC 0.978 for NT‑proBNP)</cite>.

Bedside imaging and ultrasound
- Chest X‑ray: noncardiogenic (dengue‑like) edema shows bilateral, diffuse, patchy infiltrates with air bronchograms and “Kerley B” lines; cardiogenic edema shows cephalization, Hampton’s lines, and prominent Kerley B lines with cardiomegaly. Distribution and signs of elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure are key discriminators. <cite id="52db8305-2">Cardiogenic pulmonary edema exhibits cephalization and broad vascular pedicle with peri-bronchovascular “septal” (Kerley B) lines; noncardiogenic edema presents diffuse bilateral infiltrates with air bronchograms, not specific but characteristic</cite>. 
- Lung ultrasound (POCUS) is more sensitive than symptoms/radiography for cardiogenic edema and quantifies extravascular lung water via B‑lines. It can also detect pleural fluid and assess IVC collapsibility to gauge fluid responsiveness. <cite id="52db8305-2">Transthoracic ultrasound detects pulmonary edema via B‑lines representing alveolar‑interstitial fluid; B‑line number correlates with extravascular lung water and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure</cite> and <cite id="52db8305-0">BLUE/FALLS protocols use B‑lines to differentiate cardiogenic from other shock; POCUS of IVC and lung ultrasound can guide fluid management in dengue</cite>. 
- Anterior chest alone can miss lateral zone pathology; include lateral decubitus views to reduce sensitivity loss in ED settings. <cite id="52db8305-1">Limiting lung ultrasound to the anterior chest misses up to 16.5% of ADHF cases; adding lateral views improves detection</cite>. 
- Distribution matters: diffuse B‑lines across multiple zones support noncardiogenic edema (capillary leak/ARDS), focal B‑lines and pleural effusion with septic features suggest infection; cardiogenic patterns localize to dependent bases with IVC distension and cardiomegaly on CXR. <cite id="52db8305-4">Diffuse multiple B‑lines appear in noncardiogenic edema (ARDS, pneumonia); focal B‑lines are common in pneumonia, contusion, infarction, malignancy</cite> and <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">clinical fluid accumulation (effusions) is a dengue warning sign with marked hemoconcentration</cite>.

Clinical reasoning at initial presentation
- Suggestive of dengue‑induced capillary leak/pulmonary edema:
  - Early post‑febrile (within 5–10 days), febrile chart shows typical DF course; new tachypnea/dyspnea with hypoxemia; hypotension/postural drop; abdominal pain or hepatomegaly; persistent vomiting; lethargy; mucosal bleeding; rising hematocrit (20% within 6–8 h) with falling platelets; pleural/ascites on exam or FAST-like ultrasound; CXR shows bilateral patchy infiltrates with air bronchograms; ultrasound shows diffuse B‑lines across lung fields with low IVC pressure; BNP modestly elevated or not diagnostic for heart failure. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">Dengue pulmonary edema occurred during days 5–6 post‑onset with marked hemoconcentration and profound shock</cite>, <cite id="39a6fdf1-4">pleural effusion appears early in critical phase from capillary leak</cite>, <cite id="39a6fdf1-1">postural hypotension predicts severe dengue with high sensitivity/specificity</cite>, <cite id="7a79cc2d-2">hematocrit rise of 20% confirms plasma leakage; platelet drop precedes it</cite>, <cite id="52db8305-2">noncardiogenic edema patterns on imaging</cite>, <cite id="52db8305-0">lung ultrasound and IVC assessment guide fluid therapy</cite>.
- Suggestive of iatrogenic fluid overload:
  - Recent transfusion(s) with fresh plasma/packed cells or large crystalloids; positive fluid balance of liters in 24–48 hours; tachypnea with hypoxemia despite or after diuretics; rising JVP/neck vein distension, distant heart sounds, bibasilar crackles; CXR shows patchy infiltrates with signs of cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion; lung ultrasound shows prominent B‑lines with possible pleural fluid and non‑collapsible IVC; BNP markedly elevated with clinical sepsis/ARDS superimposed. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">Effusion‑related fluid overload caused pulmonary edema on day 16 in a patient with malignant pleural effusion</cite>, <cite id="52db8305-0">inappropriate fluid therapy increases fluid overload; POCUS can detect fluid overload signs</cite>, <cite id="52db8305-2">IVC collapse indicates fluid overload; ultrasound detects pleural effusions and evaluates IVC</cite>.

Workup and early monitoring plan
- Immediate: oxygenation/saturation, O2 requirement, BP with posture, HR, capillary refill, urine output, hematocrit vs baseline, platelets, white blood cell count with neutrophils/bandemia, and a focused physical and abdominal exam. <cite id="39a6fdf1-1">Postural hypotension’s diagnostic performance supports its use early in dengue</cite> and <cite id="39a6fdf1-3">rise in hematocrit has low sensitivity but high specificity for severe dengue</cite>.
- Imaging: chest radiograph to assess infiltrates and distribution; if equivocal, bedside lung ultrasound with anterior and lateral views, measurement of B‑line counts, pleural effusion search, and IVC collapsibility. <cite id="52db8305-2">B‑line number correlates with extravascular water and predicts outcomes</cite> and <cite id="52db8305-4">diffuse B‑lines favor noncardiogenic edema</cite>. 
- Laboratories: repeat hematocrit/platelets every 4–6 hours; consider BNP/NT‑proBNP if available to quantify cardiac stress; obtain blood cultures if sepsis is suspected based on warning signs. <cite id="52db8305-0">NT‑proBNP levels correlate with B‑lines and identify cardiogenic pulmonary edema</cite> and <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">bacteremia is an important warning sign with high leukocytosis</cite>.

Differential pitfalls and how to avoid
- Overdiagnosing plasma leakage when fluid overload is present: maintain strict fluid balance charts; hold transfusions unless for shock; favor restrictive transfusion thresholds; use POCUS to guide both resuscitation and de‑resuscitation. <cite id="52db8305-0">Inappropriate fluid therapy increases congestive heart failure risk; inverted “V” titration with POCUS reduces overload risk</cite>. 
- Under‑recognizing cardiogenic decompensation in dengue: do not rely solely on hematocrit; evaluate for sepsis, MI, or pre‑existing HF; use BNP and ultrasound to detect cardiac etiologies. <cite id="52db8305-0">Cardiogenic shock in dengue has elevated NT‑proBNP with >30 B‑lines and can mimic plasma leakage</cite>. 
- Under‑recognizing dengue plasma leakage: track hematocrit trends and warning signs; do not wait for massive hemoconcentration. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">Plasma leakage can be suspected even without extreme hematocrit elevation if effusions and hypotensive episodes occur</cite> and <cite id="39a6fdf1-2">significant hematocrit rise may be absent if early fluid intervention alters physiology</cite>.

Practical bedside algorithm at initial presentation
1) Ask history: febrile course, dengue exposure, transfusions/IV fluids in last 24–48 h, baseline cardiac disease. Measure 24 h intake/output. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">Differentiate dengue edema (early post‑febrile) from effusion‑related overload (later with clear exposure)</cite> and <cite id="52db8305-0">track fluid balance and use POCUS to prevent overload</cite>. 
2) Hemodynamics: BP with posture, pulse, JVP, cap refill. Identify postural drop or narrow pulse pressure. <cite id="39a6fdf1-1">Postural fall in SBP >10.33% strongly predicts severe dengue</cite>. 
3) Warning signs: abdominal pain/persistent vomiting, lethargy, mucosal bleeding, hepatomegaly, fluid accumulation, hematocrit trajectory. <cite id="39a6fdf1-0">WHO warning signs define risk of plasma leakage/severe dengue</cite> and <cite id="7a79cc2d-2">20% hematocrit rise and platelet drop guide plasma leakage assessment</cite>. 
4) Imaging: chest X‑ray and bedside lung ultrasound (anterior + lateral). Assess distribution and presence of pleural fluid; count B‑lines; evaluate IVC. <cite id="52db8305-2">Diffuse B‑lines across lung zones favor noncardiogenic edema; add lateral views to reduce missed cardiogenic cases</cite> and <cite id="52db8305-0">IVC ultrasound detects fluid overload; B‑line counts correlate with NT‑proBNP</cite>.

Title: Fatal Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever in Adults: Emphasizing the Evolutionary Pre-fatal Clinical and Laboratory Manifestations
Snippet: The pulmonary edema developed in the 2 patients (patients 5 and 8) with DSS on day 5 and day 6 after the dengue onset, respectively, was accompanied by a concurrent marked hemoconcentration (see Table S1 for details) suggested continuous fluid leakage from the intravascular compartment to the extravascular compartment and the lung alveolar space in particular, leading to profound shock and pulmonary edema. In contrast, the pulmonary edema developed on day 16 in patients 4 who had an underlying lung cancer with malignant pleural effusion obviously resulted from fluid overload. 

The latest WHO scheme classified dengue in terms of clinical severity as severe dengue (i.e., presence of severe bleeding, severe plasma leak and/or severe organ involvement) or non-severe dengue; for practical reasons, patients with non-severe dengue were further separated into those with warning signs (i.e., abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy/restless, liver enlargement, and increase in hematocrit in concurrent with rapid decrease in platelet count) and those without them [18]. Severe dengue patients with aggravated plasma leak and/or bleeding necessitate aggressive fluid resuscitation and additional blood transfusion as necessary, while non-severe dengue patients with warning sign(s) require strict observation, appropriate medical intervention and intravenous hydration, as they are at high risk for evolving into critical phase-severe dengue [18]. In addition to the aforementioned ones, our data suggest that leukocytosis, bandemia and hypothermia may be warning signs of severe dengue. From the pathophysiological point of view, leukocytosis and/or bandemia indicates a superimposing bacterial infection and/or other stressful stimuli [19]. Our data suggested that massive GI bleeding (33.3%) and bacteremia (25%) be the major causes of DHF patients' prefatal leukocytosis.

Title: Postural fall in systolic blood pressure is a useful warning sign in dengue fever
Snippet: Background Capillary leak is the hallmark of development of severe dengue. A rise in haematocrit has been a major warning sign in WHO guidelines. Postural hypotension, which could reflect the intravascular volume reduction in capillary leak has been noted as warning sign in CDC and Pan American Health Organisation guidelines. We evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of postural hypotension as a marker of development of severe dengue. Methods 150 patients admitted with dengue fever were recruited in this prospective observational study. Diagnostic accuracy of conventional warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, liver enlargement, increasing hematocrit with decreasing platelets) and postural hypotension was evaluated. Results 23 (15.3%) subjects developed severe dengue. Multiple logistic regression analysis showed that ascites/pleural effusion and postural fall in systolic blood pressure of >10.33% had odds ratio of 5.024(95%CI:1.11 – 22.75) and 11.369 (95% CI:2.27 – 56.87), respectively. Other parameters did not reach statistical significance. Sensitivity and specificity of ascites/pleural effusion were 82.6% and 88.2% for development of severe dengue whereas postural fall in systolic blood pressure had sensitivity and specificity of 87% and 82.7%. Conclusions These findings present a strong case for including postural hypotension as a warning sign in patients with dengue fever, especially in resource limited settings.

Title: Usefulness of World Health Organization (WHO) dengue case classifications in a Sri Lankan clinical setting
Snippet: Previous studies have also noted similar findings and found some non-dengue related viral infections also to have similar manifestations 19,[26][27][28][29] . 

The percentage increase in haematocrit is an accurate indicator of vascular permeability and plasma leakage. Significant rise was seen in 36 (46.2%) of dengue fever patients and 20 (71%) of DHF patients. Plasma leakage was suspected in other 8 DHF patients without a significant rise in PCV, due to the presence of effusions and hypotensive episodes that responded to fluid therapy. It is likely that the effect of early fluid intervention would have changed the natural course of the illness and thus produced this mixed picture. It was also reported in previous studies that in some cases the fluid leakage does not achieve a high degree haemoconcentration even if the patient is in shock 10 . In some DF patients the rise of PCV could have been due to dehydration as a result of poor intake and vomiting. Further, the absence of pre-morbid PCV levels prevented us obtaining the accurate values in some patients. As mean population PCVs for Sri Lankan males and females are not available, the standard PCV values considered by us (males, 40 and females, 35) may be too high, as poor socioeconomic conditions found in developing countries lead to anaemia and a low PCV as described in several Indian studies 30,31 . 

Only five patients in our cohort would have been classified as having DHF using the 1997 WHO dengue classification. Not performing tourniquet test would have been a contributory factor for this trend. Thus, in clinical practice, we found that DHF does not necessarily fulfill all four WHO criteria recommended for the diagnosis. 

The WHO 2009 revised case classification use warning signs to classify patients into dengue, dengue with warning signs and severe dengue. The presence or absence of warning signs was available for all 106 patients. It was possible to classify all patients into the three categories; 19 (17.95%) without warning signs, 82 (77.4%) with warning signs and 5 (4.7%) severe dengue. Majority of patients had dengue with warning signs.

Title: Postural fall in systolic blood pressure is a useful warning sign in dengue fever
Snippet: We have studied 150 inpatients with dengue and evaluated the diagnostic performance of warning signs and postural hypotension. Fluid accumulation in cavities and postural fall in SBP of >10.33% were found to have good sensitivity and  specificity. Multiple logistic regression showed that other warning signs did not have significant adjusted odds ratio for the development of severe dengue compared to ascites/pleural effusion and postural fall in SBP. Based on decision tree analysis, we developed a model to identify patients with high risk of progression to severe dengue utilizing simple clinical tools (postural hypotension and pleural effusion/ascites). Diagnostic odds ratio of the model is 53.9, making the decision tree a very good diagnostic tool for ruling out the risk of progression to severe dengue. This model performed well both in the development and validation cohort confirming good internal validity. 

Severe dengue develops in about 5-15% of patients with dengue fever. 2 Capillary leak is a unique and major pathogenetic mechanism in the development of severe dengue. Hence, markers of capillary leak like rising hematocrit and fluid accumulation in cavities have been part of dengue management protocols. WHO has identified seven warning signs for severe dengue: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, liver enlargement, increasing hematocrit with decreasing platelets. These markers have been used extensively to triage patients with dengue fever to identify those at higher risk of developing severe dengue. Severe dengue has high mortality of nearly 20% which can be brought down to nearly 1% of patients if identified early and managed appropriately. 6 Recently, many studies have been published evaluating the performance of these parameters in predicting severe dengue. In a study published from Malaysia, 700 patients were studied to evaluate the diagnostic performance of warning signs for association with severe dengue. Though specificity was good, sensitivity was suboptimal. Sensitivity of rise in hematocrit was 0.29 which was similar to our study (0.13) and specificity was above 90%. 2 Capillary leak occurs secondary to damage of endothelial cell-to-cell junction.

Title: Clinical and Hematological Parameters as the Predictors of Shock in Dengue Infection
Snippet: The cases of DSS were found in 30% of 110 patients with dengue infection who met the inclusion criteria. This is not much different from the DSS cases in several other studies ranging 30-40%. 7,12 In this study identified several DSS predictors indicating warning signs of dengue infection listed in WHO guidelines. Warning signs are a collection of signs and symptoms that precede shock manifestations, enabling them to be used as a prognosis for DSS cases. Such signs appear at the end of the acute phase because of increased capillary permeability. 8 Endothelial dysfunction leads to capillary permeability due to the release of inflammatory mediators triggered by proinflammatory cytokines. Such cytokines are produced by the cells infected with dengue virus. 14 ccumulation of fluid in tissues, including ascites and pleural effusion, is a manifestation of plasma leakage due to increased capillary permeability. This clinical sign appears at the beginning of the critical phase. 8 In this study, pleural effusion had a highly significant correlation with DSS cases in children and was an important predictor factor (OR=31.45). These results are consistent with several previous studies. 12,13 he incident of gastrointestinal bleeding in this study was more common in subjects with DSS than in non-shock cases, making it a strong predictor factor with OR=32.62. This finding is in line with other studies. 7,12,13,15 Gastrointestinal bleeding is closely related to thrombocytopenia in severe dengue infection. 16,17 The degree of severity of thrombocytopenia is directly proportional to the severity of hemorrhagic manifestations. In dengue patients, platelet counts of <50,000/ µL have a significant association with severe bleeding. 18 3]15 Abdominal pain is an early indicator of increased capillary permeability and is a prognostic factor for predicting the severity of dengue infection. 11,16 t can be caused by gastrointestinal bleeding, hepatomegaly, or tissue hypoxia due to insufficient visceral blood supply during the condition of pre-dengue and dengue shock. 10

Title: Decreased sensitivity of lung ultrasound limited to the anterior chest in emergency department diagnosis of cardiogenic pulmonary edema: a retrospective analysis
Snippet: PurposesB-lines are vertical echogenic artifacts seen on lung ultrasound that allow bedside diagnosis of pulmonary edema. Title: Fatal Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever in Adults: Emphasizing the Evolutionary Pre-fatal Clinical and Laboratory Manifestations
Snippet: The pulmonary edema developed in the 2 patients (patients 5 and 8) with DSS on day 5 and day 6 after the dengue onset, respectively, was accompanied by a concurrent marked hemoconcentration (see Table S1 for details) suggested continuous fluid leakage from the intravascular compartment to the extravascular compartment and the lung alveolar space in particular, leading to profound shock and pulmonary edema. In contrast, the pulmonary edema developed on day 16 in patients 4 who had an underlying lung cancer with malignant pleural effusion obviously resulted from fluid overload. 

The latest WHO scheme classified dengue in terms of clinical severity as severe dengue (i.e., presence of severe bleeding, severe plasma leak and/or severe organ involvement) or non-severe dengue; for practical reasons, patients with non-severe dengue were further separated into those with warning signs (i.e., abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy/restless, liver enlargement, and increase in hematocrit in concurrent with rapid decrease in platelet count) and those without them [18]. Severe dengue patients with aggravated plasma leak and/or bleeding necessitate aggressive fluid resuscitation and additional blood transfusion as necessary, while non-severe dengue patients with warning sign(s) require strict observation, appropriate medical intervention and intravenous hydration, as they are at high risk for evolving into critical phase-severe dengue [18]. In addition to the aforementioned ones, our data suggest that leukocytosis, bandemia and hypothermia may be warning signs of severe dengue. From the pathophysiological point of view, leukocytosis and/or bandemia indicates a superimposing bacterial infection and/or other stressful stimuli [19]. Our data suggested that massive GI bleeding (33.3%) and bacteremia (25%) be the major causes of DHF patients' prefatal leukocytosis.

Title: Revisiting the fluid requirement during the critical phase of dengue: Does it actually follow a bell-shaped curve?
Snippet: Plasma leakage due to a transient increase in capillary permeability is the hallmark of dengue haemorrhagic fever. There is no specific antiviral agent for dengue. Therefore, the mainstay of management during the plasma leakage phase is the judicious use of intravenous fluid to ensure adequate organ perfusion and to prevent fluid overload. The current practice guidelines for dengue are empirical. They are mostly based on expert opinions. The rates and amounts of fluid to be administered during the critical phase of the disease have not been studied in randomised controlled trials. It is hypothesised that the rate of fluid leakage during the critical phase follows a bell-shaped curve. Based on this concept, both WHO and Sri Lankan guidelines recommend starting fluid at a lower rate, increasing the rate until the midpoint of the CP, and gradually reducing the infusion rate thereafter. However, the authors believe that the more fluid you give during the critical phase, the more will leak out into the third space. Thus increasing the complications of fluid overload without improving the effective plasma volume. Therefore, administering fluids at an escalating rate may be superfluous and could result in fluid overload.

Title: Risk prediction for severe disease and better diagnostic accuracy in early dengue infection; the Colombo dengue study
Snippet: The outcomes assessed in this study were plasma leakage and severe dengue. Plasma leakage was identified according to the National Guidelines on dengue management [13]. In brief, bed-side hematocrit assessments were done at intervals of 6 to 8 h to demonstrate a rise of 20% from baseline. Alternatively, ultrasound evidence (pleural effusions, peri-cholecystic fluid or ascites) was also confirmatory for plasma leakage. Platelet count was used as a surrogate marker to guide the timing of ultrasound examinations as a drop-in platelet count below 100,000/mm3 is observed to precede plasma leakage by 24-48 h [13]. Patients within this time window were examined by ultrasound scans twice daily. Severe dengue was defined according the previously published criteria by World Health Organization (WHO). This included patients with plasma leakage plus shock or fluid overload, severe bleeding or severe organ impairment [19].

Title: Fluid Management in Dengue -Insights from Bedside
Snippet: Dengue fever, a prevalent tropical viral illness transmitted by mosquitoes, poses a substantial burden on healthcare systems in Southeast Asia. Despite the increase in case density annually there is a noticeable downward trend in mortality rates in Sri Lanka. The pathophysiological hallmark of severe dengue is plasma leakage, leading to potentially life-threatening complications such as shock and organ failure. Key aspects of clinical care include early recognition of warning signs, monitoring of clinical parameters, and tailoring fluid therapy to individual patient needs. Optimizing fluid management is essential for reducing morbidity and mortality associated with severe dengue infection. Key decisions on fluid management are individualized with intense monitoring of vital parameters. The amount and type of fluid administered to maintain adequate perfusion while preventing fluid overload are based on the bed side clinical and sonographic assessment. This case-based discussion provides an overview of current fluid management strategies in various clinical stages of dengue highlighting the common pitfalls that may arise during management of complicated dengue patients. It is of utmost importance that we acquire the insight into the judicious fluid management during critical phase of dengue to minimize morbidity and mortality.

snippet.text: The outcomes assessed in this study were plasma leakage and severe dengue. Plasma leakage was identified according to the National Guidelines on dengue management [13]. In brief, bed-side hematocrit assessments were done at intervals of 6 to 8 h to demonstrate a rise of 20% from baseline. Alternatively, ultrasound evidence (pleural effusions, peri-cholecystic fluid or ascites) was also confirmatory for plasma leakage. Platelet count was used as a surrogate marker to guide the timing of ultrasound examinations as a drop-in platelet count below 100,000/mm3 is observed to precede plasma leakage by 24-48 h [13]. Patients within this time window were examined by ultrasound scans twice daily. Severe dengue was defined according the previously published criteria by World Health Organization (WHO). This included patients with plasma leakage plus shock or fluid overload, severe bleeding or severe organ impairment [19].

snippet.text:
Dengue fever, a prevalent tropical viral illness transmitted by mosquitoes, poses a substantial burden on healthcare systems in Southeast Asia. Despite the increase in case density annually there is a noticeable downward trend in mortality rates in Sri Lanka. The pathophysiological hallmark of severe dengue is plasma leakage, leading to potentially life-threatening complications such as shock and organ failure. Key aspects of clinical care include early recognition of warning signs, monitoring of clinical parameters, and tailoring fluid therapy to individual patient needs. Optimizing fluid management is essential for reducing morbidity and mortality associated with severe dengue infection. Key decisions on fluid management are individualized with intense monitoring of vital parameters. The amount and type of fluid administered to maintain adequate perfusion while preventing fluid overload are based on the bed side clinical and sonographic assessment. This case-based discussion provides an overview of current fluid management strategies in various clinical stages of dengue highlighting the common pitfalls that may arise during management of complicated dengue patients. It is of utmost importance that we acquire the insight into the judicious fluid management during critical phase of dengue to minimize morbidity and mortality. 
Bangladesh J Medicine 2024; Vol. 35, No. 2, Supplementation: 130-131

documents.snippet:
The pulmonary edema developed in the 2 patients (patients 5 and 8) with DSS on day 5 and day 6 after the dengue onset, respectively, was accompanied by a concurrent marked hemoconcentration (see Table S1 for details) suggested continuous fluid leakage from the intravascular compartment to the extravascular compartment and the lung alveolar space in particular, leading to profound shock and pulmonary edema. In contrast, the pulmonary edema developed on day 16 in patients 4 who had an underlying lung cancer with malignant pleural effusion obviously resulted from fluid overload. 

The latest WHO scheme classified dengue in terms of clinical severity as severe dengue (i.e., presence of severe bleeding, severe plasma leak and/or severe organ involvement) or non-severe dengue; for practical reasons, patients with non-severe dengue were further separated into those with warning signs (i.e., abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy/restless, liver enlargement, and increase in hematocrit in concurrent with rapid decrease in platelet count) and those without them [18]. Severe dengue patients with aggravated plasma leak and/or bleeding necessitate aggressive fluid resuscitation and additional blood transfusion as necessary, while non-severe dengue patients with warning sign(s) require strict observation, appropriate medical intervention and intravenous hydration, as they are at high risk for evolving into critical phase-severe dengue [18]. In addition to the aforementioned ones, our data suggest that leukocytosis, bandemia and hypothermia may be warning signs of severe dengue. From the pathophysiological point of view, leukocytosis and/or bandemia indicates a superimposing bacterial infection and/or other stressful stimuli [19]. Our data suggested that massive GI bleeding (33.3%) and bacteremia (25%) be the major causes of DHF patients' prefatal leukocytosis.

documents.title: Revisiting the fluid requirement during the critical phase of dengue: Does it actually follow a bell-shaped curve?
documents.snippet: Plasma leakage due to a transient increase in capillary permeability is the hallmark of dengue haemorrhagic fever. There is no specific antiviral agent for dengue. Therefore, the mainstay of management during the plasma leakage phase is the judicious use of intravenous fluid to ensure adequate organ perfusion and to prevent fluid overload. The current practice guidelines for dengue are empirical. They are mostly based on expert opinions. The rates and amounts of fluid to be administered during the critical phase of the disease have not been studied in randomised controlled trials. It is hypothesised that the rate of fluid leakage during the critical phase follows a bell-shaped curve. Based on this concept, both WHO and Sri Lankan guidelines recommend starting fluid at a lower rate, increasing the rate until the midpoint of the CP, and gradually reducing the infusion rate thereafter. However, the authors believe that the more fluid you give during the critical phase, the more will leak out into the third space. Thus increasing the complications of fluid overload without improving the effective plasma volume. Therefore, administering fluids at an escalating rate may be superfluous and could result in fluid overload.

attempts.answer:
Overview and challenge
Dengue-associated severe disease is driven by abrupt increases in vascular permeability (“capillary leak”) around day 3–7 of illness, causing fluid accumulation and hemodynamic instability; in contrast, iatrogenic fluid overload produces pulmonary edema by increasing left atrial pressure with or without concurrent capillary leak. At initial ED presentation—before any treatment—the key is to rapidly distinguish a virus-triggered leak syndrome with hypovolemic shock risk and fluid-reserve “repletion” needs from a state where the primary mechanism of edema is volume excess or cardiac dysfunction. <cite id="e01fcaeb-3">The critical phase usually lasts 24–48 hours with increased vascular permeability leading to fluid leakage and complications such as pleural effusions, ascites, shock, and multi-organ failure</cite>. <cite id="e01fcaeb-2">Uncontrolled IV fluids in dengue with permeability can rapidly cause hypervolemia, fluid accumulation in the lungs, and pulmonary edema</cite>. <cite id="e01fcaeb-1">Guidelines emphasize close monitoring with serial hematocrits and careful fluid management during dengue shock, balancing hemodynamic stability against iatrogenic volume overload</cite>. <cite id="43ea26bb-0">Pulmonary edema can be broadly categorized into cardiogenic (elevated filling pressures) and noncardiogenic (fluid accumulation without elevated wedge pressure), and rapid identification is essential for etiologic-directed therapy</cite>.

Step 1: History and epidemiology (to anchor dengue-induced leak vs iatrogenic overload)
- Exposure and timeline: ask travel to endemic areas, mosquito bite exposure, recent dengue/flu-like illness, defervescence timing, and any “warning signs” at presentation. <cite id="ad5819b0-0">Dengue with warning signs includes abdominal pain/tenderness, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, liver enlargement, and hematocrit rise with falling platelets</cite>. <cite id="ad5819b0-0">Severe forms include hypovolemic shock with plasma leakage, fluid accumulation with respiratory distress, severe bleeding, and severe organ involvement</cite>. <cite id="ad5819b0-2">Abdominal pain and persistent vomiting are among the earliest warning signs; sudden hypotension, vomiting, severe abdominal pain, and restlessness often occur on the day of deterioration</cite>. 
- History of recent transfusions or massive IV fluids within hours to days can mimic dengue leak but is iatrogenic; contrast with community-acquired dengue. <cite id="e01fcaeb-2">Uncontrolled IV volume replacement in dengue vascular permeability can precipitate hypervolemia, respiratory distress, and pulmonary edema</cite>.
- Overlap: myocarditis/heart failure may be triggered by dengue; history of chest pain, palpitations, syncope, or prior cardiomyopathy raises the possibility of cardiogenic edema superimposed on leak. <cite id="e01fcaeb-0">Dengue infection is associated with endothelial dysfunction, hypovolemia-induced cardiac stress, and myocarditis/myocardial dysfunction; recognizing cardiac involvement in dengue with capillary leakage is crucial for timely management</cite>.

Step 2: Hemodynamics and early “danger signs” (the fastest bedside clues to leak vs overload)
- Look for shock physiology out of proportion to loss, tachycardia with narrow pulse pressure, and unstable BP. <cite id="e01fcaeb-2">Because of increased peripheral vascular resistance, dengue shock frequently manifests a narrow pulse pressure with normal systolic BP; shock may not be recognized until late</cite>. <cite id="e01fcaeb-3">Increased vascular permeability peaks on days 3–7, after which fluid reabsorbs over 24–48 hours</cite>. 
- Fluid-reserve vs overload signals:
  - Capillary leak: hypotension or hypoperfusion with low CVP/PAOP, tachycardia, cool periphery, but normal or low PCWP is misleading if not measured; hematocrit rising or rebounding suggests plasma leakage. <cite id="e01fcaeb-1">Dengue shock usually occurs around defervescence; serial hematocrits are used to guide fluid management because leakage severity is indirectly reflected by hematocrit changes</cite>. <cite id="e01fcaeb-2">Evidence of plasma leakage includes hematocrit rise ≥20% above baseline, drop after volume replacement equal to 20% of baseline, and signs such as pleural effusion, ascites, and hypoproteinemia</cite>. 
  - Iatrogenic overload: hypotension with elevated CVP/PAOP, JVD, elevated BP or pulsus paradoxus early, and signs of pulmonary congestion. <cite id="43ea26bb-0">Cardiogenic pulmonary edema reflects elevated cardiac filling pressures; noncardiogenic edema occurs without elevated wedge pressures</cite>. <cite id="43ea26bb-1">Cardiogenic edema classically shows bilateral perihilar opacities, Kerley B lines, pleural effusions, and heart enlargement on CXR</cite>. 
- Early warning: dengue with “abdominal pain, vomiting, lethargy, and fluid accumulation” is at high risk to deteriorate; treat as severe dengue and avoid fluid loading. <cite id="ad5819b0-0">Abdominal pain/tenderness, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, lethargy, and rising hematocrit with falling platelets identify dengue with warning signs</cite>. <cite id="ad5819b0-2">These warning signs often appear on day of deterioration, with sudden hypotension, vomiting, and abdominal pain being common</cite>.

Step 3: Physical exam clues to organ involvement (leak vs overload)
- Cutaneous and mucosal bleeding, petechiae, positive tourniquet test, pleural/ascitic fluid, and periorbital “shininess” from hypoproteinemia point to capillary leak. <cite id="e02fcaeb-2">Signs of plasma leakage include pleural effusion, ascites, and hypoproteinemia</cite>. <cite id="e01fcaeb-0">Dengue infection is associated with capillary leak manifestations such as pleural effusion, ascites, and vascular permeability</cite>. 
- Cardiogenic overload often shows jugular venous distension, basal crackles, third heart sound, and peripheral edema; in dengue shock, early hypotension and tachycardia may mask classic heart failure signs. <cite id="e01fcaeb-2">Dengue shock may present with narrow pulse pressure and normal systolic BP, making circulatory failure hard to recognize</cite>. <cite id="43ea26bb-1">Cardiogenic edema CXR shows enlarged heart and pleural effusions; noncardiogenic edema lacks prominent heart enlargement</cite>.

Step 4: Initial labs and early markers of capillary leak and coagulopathy
- Hemoglobin/platelets, hematocrit, and quick coagulation screen. Rising hematocrit or late drop after fluid resuscitation suggests ongoing plasma leakage; thrombocytopenia with bleeding points to dengue/DISS. <cite id="e01fcaeb-2">Hematocrit rise ≥20% above baseline or drop after volume replacement equal to 20% of baseline indicates plasma leakage; coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia are typical</cite>. <cite id="e01fcaeb-1">Hematocrit changes reflect leakage but become unreliable once parenteral fluids are given</cite>. 
- Infection/inflammation markers and liver enzymes (AST/ALT). <cite id="ad5819b0-1">Abdominal pain is associated with liver involvement in dengue; presence of multiple warning signs predicts severe dengue</cite>. <cite id="ad5819b0-1">Abdominal pain and persistent vomiting are strong warning signs; raised AST levels correlate with abdominal pain and liver involvement</cite>. 
- Contrast with iatrogenic overload: labs may show volume overload markers (B-type natriuretic peptide can be elevated in both heart failure and high-capacity fluid resuscitation; treat as supportive rather than diagnostic).

Step 5: Imaging and early hemodynamic interrogation
- Chest radiography: position the edema pattern on the spectrum of cardiogenic vs noncardiogenic processes. <cite id="43ea26bb-1">Cardiogenic edema typically shows bilateral perihilar “bat-wing” opacities, Kerley B lines, pleural effusions, and an enlarged heart; noncardiogenic edema presents with bilateral infiltrates without marked heart enlargement or effusions</cite>. 
- Point-of-care ultrasound and early echocardiography: use bedside lung ultrasound (B-LUS) to detect pulmonary edema and its distribution and POCUS for IVC/AAV diameter to assess volume responsiveness; in severe dengue with capillary leak, IVC may be collapsed despite shock from plasma loss, whereas overload shows elevated CVP with pericardial effusion in some settings. <cite id="43ea26bb-0">Bedside ultrasound and echocardiography are part of ED workup for pulmonary edema</cite>. <cite id="43ea26bb-3">Echocardiography can differentiate cardiac vs noncardiac origin of pulmonary edema when bedside criteria are unclear</cite>. <cite id="43ea26bb-4">Clinical and echocardiographic markers (e.g., elevated central venous pressure, ventricular strain) help distinguish cardiogenic from noncardiogenic edema and can be critical in TACO vs TRALI differentiation</cite>. 
- In dengue, early POCUS may show hepatomegaly, pleural effusions, and collapsing/normal LV function with low stroke volumes in shock; avoid fluid if evidence of overload. <cite id="e01fcaeb-2">Respiratory distress may occur abruptly in dengue vascular leak; uncontrolled IV fluids can turn shock into pulmonary edema</cite>. <cite id="e01fcaeb-0">Endothelial dysfunction and hypovolemia-induced cardiac stress in dengue can cause myocardial injury, so POCUS/echo should assess for concurrent cardiac dysfunction</cite>.

Step 6: Distinguishing features and pitfalls (overlap and time)
- Time course and precipitants: dengue leak is time-stamped by fever resolution on days 3–7; rapid respiratory distress after IV fluids suggests iatrogenic overload in a febrile, thrombocytopenic patient with pleural effusion. <cite id="e01fcaeb-3">The leak phase peaks on days 3–7 and resolves over 24–48 hours</cite>. <cite id="e01fcaeb-2">Without careful fluid management, dengue patients may slip from shock to pulmonary edema</cite>. 
- Overlap syndromes: myocarditis/heart failure superimposed on capillary leak can present with pulmonary edema, tachycardia, hypotension, and elevated troponin; treat as cardiogenic until proven otherwise, but consider dengue myocardial involvement and proceed cautiously with fluids and inotropes. <cite id="e01fcaeb-0">Dengue infection is linked to myocarditis and myocardial dysfunction, contributing to heart failure in the setting of capillary leakage</cite>. 
- Diagnostic dilemma when warning signs are absent: early leakage can be subtle. <cite id="e01fcaeb-2">Clinical signs and symptoms often occur late; severe ongoing leakage may require invasive monitoring</cite>. <cite id="e01fcaeb-1">Serial hematocrits indirectly reflect leakage severity but become unreliable once fluids are given</cite>. In such cases, rapid recheck, early capnography/BP trends, repeated hematocrit/platelets, and cautious small-volume “resuscitation with reassessment” can differentiate responders from non-responders. <cite id="e01fcaeb-1">Dengue shock management over 24–48 hours balances hemodynamic stability against iatrogenic overload; frequent reassessment guides therapy</cite>.

Practical initial ED algorithm (before any treatment)
1) Stabilize airway, breathing, circulation:
   - Supplement oxygen; prepare for noninvasive or invasive ventilation if severe respiratory distress. 
   - If hypotensive with shock but low perfusion, prepare fluids; if high perfusion with pulmonary edema and elevated CVP, avoid fluid. <cite id="e01fcaeb-2">Shock in dengue may be masked by narrow pulse pressure; careful clinical recognition is needed</cite>. <cite id="43ea26bb-0">Cardiogenic edema reflects elevated filling pressures; noncardiogenic occurs without elevated wedge pressure</cite>. 
2) Rapid deconfusion:
   - Dengue: fever resolving, thrombocytopenia, bleeding signs, pleural effusion, abdominal pain with vomiting, lethargy. <cite id="ad5819b0-0">Abdominal pain/tenderness, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, lethargy, rising hematocrit, and falling platelets</cite>. 
   - Iatrogenic overload: recent transfusion/massive IV in a febrile, thrombocytopenic patient; precipitous respiratory distress after fluid. <cite id="e01fcaeb-2">Uncontrolled IV fluids can precipitate hypervolemia and pulmonary edema in dengue</cite>. 
3) Early labs and monitoring:
   - CBC (platelets), coagulation (PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen), electrolytes, renal function, BUN/creatinine, troponin, GGT/LFTs; repeat hematocrit in 1–2 hours to test fluid responsiveness. <cite id="e01fcaeb-2">Signs of plasma leakage include hematocrit changes and coagulopathy</cite>. <cite id="e01fcaeb-1">Serial hematocrits guide fluid management in dengue shock</cite>. 
4) Imaging and ultrasound:
   - CXR early to identify pattern (perihilar “bat wings,” Kerley B lines vs diffuse bilateral infiltrates), and POCUS to look for pleural effusion, hepatomegaly, and to assess IVC reactivity (volume-guided approach). Echo to differentiate cardiogenic vs noncardiogenic etiology when in doubt. <cite id="43ea26bb-1">Cardiogenic edema shows bilateral perihilar opacities, Kerley B lines, pleural effusions, and heart enlargement; noncardiogenic lacks these</cite>. <cite id="e01fcaeb-2">Pleural effusion and ascites indicate plasma leakage</cite>. <cite id="43ea26bb-3">Echocardiography differentiates cardiac vs noncardiac pulmonary edema when bedside criteria are unclear</cite>. <cite id="43ea26bb-4">Central venous pressure and ventricular strain markers help distinguish cardiogenic from noncardiogenic edema</cite>. 
5) Fluid management hypothesis testing:
   - In suspected dengue capillary leak without overt overload: give very small isotonic bolus (e.g., 250–500 mL) with strict reassessment in 15–30 minutes—look for hematocrit drop, BP stabilization, urine output improvement; avoid bolus if respiratory crackles expand or BP rises into hypervolemic range. <cite id="e01fcaeb-2">Patients may rapidly slip from shock to pulmonary edema with fluids; careful observation and controlled management are required</cite>. <cite id="e01fcaeb-1">Dengue shock management over 24–48 hours requires balancing haemodynamic stability with risk of iatrogenic overload; serial assessments guide ongoing fluid management</cite>.

Snippet: Dengue infections are one of the most important vector borne diseases and are estimated to infect 390 million individuals annually [1]. The incidence of dengue has dramatically increased in many affected countries causing a significant disease burden [2]. Currently there is no licensed vaccine for its prevention, or an effective antiviral for its treatment. Management of acute dengue consists of early detection of complication and meticulous fluid management [3]. 

Dengue infection is caused by one of the four dengue virus (DV) serotypes which are closely related. Although the majority of individuals who are infected with the DV develop asymptomatic infection or an undifferentiated fever, some develop dengue fever (DF) or more severe forms of clinical disease such as dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF), dengue shock syndrome or expanded syndrome of dengue infection [3]. The initial phase of infection is characterized by a high fever (febrile phase) and coincides with the viraemia [4]. The patient may then progress to the critical phase during day 3 to 7 of illness in which there is increased vascular permeability leading to fluid leakage and shock [4,5]. Fluid leakage is the hallmark of severe dengue infection and this results in complications such as pleural effusions, ascites and if left untreated, shock and multi-organ failure [3]. The critical phase usually lasts for 24 to 48 hours and then the patient progressed to the recovery phase where the fluid is reabsorbed and the patient typically improves. Although infection of endothelial cell lines in vitro has been shown [6][7][8], due the relatively short duration of vascular leak phase in acute dengue infection, many believe that the increased vascular permeability is due to endothelial dysfunction or activation rather than damage associated with endothelial infection [9].
